subject: history
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A source's 'utility' is best understood as which of the following?
options: How useful it is for a specific historical enquiry
Whether it tells the literal truth
Whether the historian agrees with it
questions.explain: Utility is the value of a source for a particular question, so even a biased source can be highly useful.

questions.q: Why is it problematic for a historian to rely on a single uncorroborated source?
options: It is automatically a secondary source
Its claims cannot be cross-checked and may be partial or mistaken
questions.explain: Without corroboration, a lone source's accuracy and representativeness cannot be tested.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the difference between fact and interpretation?
options: Facts are only found in secondary sources
A fact is a verifiable detail; an interpretation is an argued explanation
questions.explain: Facts can be verified; interpretations are reasoned constructions built upon facts and evidence.

questions.q: When a historian uses 'contextual knowledge' to evaluate a source, they are doing what?
options: Applying their own wider knowledge of the period to test and explain the source
questions.explain: Contextual knowledge lets a historian assess whether a source is plausible, typical or partial against the broader history.

questions.q: Which of these best describes a historical 'interpretation'?
options: A historian's argument or explanation about the past
questions.explain: An interpretation is a constructed argument by a historian, shaped by evidence, selection and viewpoint.

questions.q: The 'nature' of a source refers to which of these?
options: The type or form of the source, such as a letter, speech or photograph
questions.explain: The nature of a source is its format or type, which affects what it can reliably reveal.

questions.q: Why can a deliberately biased or propagandist source still be valuable to a historian?
options: Because it removes the need for corroboration
Because it reveals the attitudes, intentions or values of its author
Because bias makes a source neutral
questions.explain: A biased source is evidence of the mindset, purpose and assumptions of those who produced it, which is itself historically revealing.

questions.q: In coursework or a historical investigation, weighing conflicting interpretations against the evidence is essential because it allows the student to do what?
options: Reach and justify a substantiated independent judgement
questions.explain: Engaging critically with rival interpretations enables a reasoned, evidence-based judgement of one's own.

questions.q: What does the 'audience' of a source mean when evaluating it?
options: The intended recipients for whom it was produced
The historians who later read it
questions.explain: Audience refers to who the author intended the source to reach, which can shape its content, tone and selectivity.

questions.q: Which approach best demonstrates a substantiated historical argument?
options: Supporting each claim with relevant, evaluated evidence
questions.explain: A substantiated argument links claims to evidence that has been weighed and explained, not merely cited.

questions.q: The danger of 'hindsight' in historical analysis refers to what?
options: Judging the past by knowledge or values unavailable at the time
questions.explain: Hindsight bias means assuming contemporaries could foresee outcomes that are only obvious to us afterwards.

questions.q: The 'purpose' of a source is best described as which of the following?
options: The reason the author produced it
The library where it is kept
The language it is written in
questions.explain: Purpose is the author's reason for creating the source, such as to persuade, record, justify or inform.

questions.q: In evaluating a primary source, the term 'provenance' refers to what?
options: The number of copies that survive
The origin, authorship and history of the source
questions.explain: Provenance concerns where a source came from, who produced it, when and under what circumstances.

questions.q: The process of checking whether different sources agree with one another is known as what?
questions.explain: Corroboration involves cross-checking sources to see whether they support, qualify or contradict each other.

questions.q: The 'tone' of a source can help a historian infer what?
options: The author's attitude or emotional stance
questions.explain: Tone, such as anger, sarcasm or reverence, signals the author's attitude and can reveal purpose and bias.

questions.q: A source described as 'typical' of its period is useful because it does what?
options: Represents wider attitudes or experiences of the time
questions.explain: A typical source can illuminate common attitudes or conditions, though typicality must still be tested against context.

questions.q: Which of these is the strongest sign that a historical interpretation is well-founded?
options: It is supported by a wide and well-evaluated evidence base
It is the most recent one published
It is written by a famous name
It agrees with our modern values
questions.explain: The strength of an interpretation rests on the breadth and rigour of the evidence and reasoning behind it.

questions.q: A private diary entry never intended for publication is often valued by historians because it may be what?
options: A primary source that needs no evaluation
Less shaped by a public audience and so more candid
questions.explain: Private writings can be more candid as the author was not addressing a public audience, though they still require evaluation.

questions.q: In historical writing, accurate referencing primarily serves to do what?
options: Allow claims to be verified and credit sources
questions.explain: Referencing enables verification of evidence and acknowledges the sources on which an argument rests.

questions.q: The historian's concept of 'attribution' involves what?
options: Rating the source out of ten
Deciding who created a source and when
questions.explain: Attribution establishes the authorship, date and origin of a source, which is fundamental to evaluating it.

questions.q: A photograph as a source has the limitation that it does which of the following?
options: Shows only a single framed moment that may be posed or selected
questions.explain: A photograph captures one chosen, framed instant and may be staged, cropped or selected, so it requires careful evaluation.

questions.q: Which statement is a fact rather than an opinion or interpretation?
options: The Treaty of 1921 was a betrayal
The Treaty was signed in December 1921
The Treaty doomed Ireland to civil war
The Treaty was the best available outcome
questions.explain: The date of signing is a verifiable fact, whereas the others are evaluative judgements.

questions.q: Which of the following is a SECONDARY source?
options: A 1916 newspaper report on the Easter Rising
A 2010 academic monograph analysing the Rising
questions.explain: A later academic work analysing events is a secondary source; the others were produced at the time.

questions.q: Why is the date of a source's creation important to its evaluation?
options: Date has no bearing on evaluation
It indicates how close the author was to events and what they could have known
Older sources are always more reliable
questions.explain: The date shows whether the author wrote as a contemporary or later, affecting knowledge, memory and hindsight.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines historical 'bias' in a source?
options: The presence of a date and author
A slant or partiality that distorts the source towards a particular view
questions.explain: Bias is a one-sided perspective that skews a source, which the historian must detect and account for rather than dismiss outright.

questions.q: Why might two historians studying the same events produce different interpretations?
options: They may use different sources, methods, questions or perspectives
Only one had access to the past
questions.explain: Historians differ because of varying evidence, approaches, ideological perspectives and the questions they choose to ask.

questions.q: An eyewitness account written decades after the event may be weakened by what?
options: The unreliability of memory and the influence of later knowledge
questions.explain: Memoirs written long afterwards can be distorted by faulty memory and by knowledge of subsequent events.

questions.q: A government's official report into a disaster might be limited as evidence because it could do what?
options: Seek to justify official actions and minimise blame
questions.explain: Official reports may be shaped by a purpose to defend the authorities, so their conclusions need critical scrutiny.

questions.q: 'Reliability' of a source differs from 'utility' because reliability concerns what?
options: How useful it is for any question
How trustworthy or accurate the source's content is
questions.explain: Reliability asks how far the source can be trusted as accurate, whereas utility asks how useful it is regardless of accuracy.

questions.q: When comparing two interpretations, identifying their 'points of emphasis' means doing what?
options: Noting what each chooses to stress or prioritise
questions.explain: Comparing emphasis reveals how historians select and weight evidence differently, shaping divergent arguments.
